name: Rice water
lead: Rice water is the cloudy, starchy liquid left after rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled. It carries starch along with small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids leached from the grain, and it can also be left to ferment for a day or two before use.[1] It has a long history of folk use in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, and it is also used as an oral fluid for diarrhoea.[1]

In appearance-focused circles it is mainly promoted as a hair rinse for length, shine and reduced breakage, and as a skin toner said to soothe and brighten the complexion.[1] A 2023 review of topical hair-loss remedies popular on TikTok, which included rice water alongside rosemary oil, onion juice and garlic gel, set out to examine the research behind such claims.[2] An encyclopedic overview notes that studies of rice water itself are limited and that claims about faster hair growth rest mainly on anecdote, such as accounts from Yao women in China.[1]
No clinical trial of rice water as a cosmetic skin or hair treatment appears in the sources reviewed. Related work exists on other rice-derived products, but it does not test rice water itself.

paras: Rice water is described as a milky suspension created when grains are rinsed or soaked in water, or when the starchy liquid is drained after boiling. Starch makes up most of the grain by weight, and the water also picks up minerals such as iron, zinc, magnesium and potassium and vitamins such as B2 and E in small quantities, with the profile varying by rice type and method.[1]

Three types are commonly distinguished: plain rice water from rinsing or soaking, boiled rice water drained from cooking, and fermented rice water, which is plain rice water left at room temperature for roughly 12 to 48 hours so that it turns slightly sour through microbial activity.[1] Proponents of the fermented form attribute extra benefit to the resulting acidity and probiotic content.[1] Rice water differs from rice milk, a blended beverage, and from rice bran water, which is extracted from the bran layer rather than the whole grain.[1]

sections.h: Use in hair and skin care
paras: As a hair rinse, rice water is said by proponents to reduce friction between strands, increase elasticity and help repair damaged hair, with the carbohydrate inositol often cited as the active component, so that hair breaks less and appears to retain length.[1] The best-known story in this area is the long hair of Yao women in China, who attribute it to regular fermented rice water rinses; the encyclopedic overview treats this as anecdotal rather than as measured evidence.[1]

On skin, rice water is used as a toner or wash with the stated aims of soothing irritation, brightening the complexion and supporting collagen, with ferulic acid and inositol named as relevant rice-derived components.[1] It is also listed among traditional lightening and skin-care ingredients in appearance-oriented communities.

Rice water is also used outside cosmetics, taken by mouth in some traditions for diarrhoea, and as a garden fertiliser.[1] Rice-based oral rehydration solutions have been studied in diarrhoeal disease, including cholera, and this literature concerns hydration rather than appearance.[3]

No studies found that test rice water as a cosmetic hair or skin treatment in humans. A 2023 narrative review in Cutis examined the evidence behind topical hair-loss remedies circulating on social media, naming rice water among them, and framed its task as assessing the research supporting those claims.[2] The encyclopedic overview states that research on rice water specifically is limited, low in quality, or concerned with other rice products such as bran extract.[1]

Studies of related rice products exist but should not be read as tests of rice water on hair or skin. A randomised, double-blind trial registered for fermented rice flour in atopic dermatitis involved 50 participants,[4] and a review and several trials have studied rice-based oral rehydration solutions for diarrhoea.[3]

Rice can accumulate arsenic from the soil and water in which it is grown, and the arsenic content of cooked rice has been studied in relation to cooking and washing methods.[5] Encyclopedic sources raise this as a consideration mainly for internal consumption of rice water and suggest low-arsenic rice varieties for that purpose.[1]

Because rice water is a starch-rich liquid, it can spoil. Guidance summarised in an encyclopedic overview says prepared rice water should be refrigerated for a few days at most and discarded if it develops an off smell or mold.[1] Topical safety data from controlled studies are not available in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Starchy rice-rinse water used as a hair and skin wash in Asian folk beauty; popular, but no trials test it for hair or skin.
card.note: Evidence is anecdotal; arsenic content of rice and spoilage are noted concerns, mainly for internal use.

quick.overview:
Rice water is the milky liquid left over when rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled. It has long been used in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, and fermented versions are popular on social media.

Proponents say it makes hair shinier, stronger and less prone to breakage, and that it brightens and soothes skin. A review of social-media hair remedies examined the evidence behind such claims, and an encyclopedic overview describes studies of rice water itself as limited, with hair growth claims resting largely on anecdote.
quick.mechanism: Rice water contains starch plus small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids. Proponents point to compounds such as inositol and ferulic acid as the reason it might smooth hair strands, reduce friction and support skin, but this mechanism has not been shown in controlled human studies of rice water.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally treated as low risk, but no controlled safety data exist. Rice can contain arsenic, which is discussed mainly for drinking rice water, and prepared rice water can spoil if stored for long.
